rv.q: A rhythm takes hold, a communal sense of purpose and shared pulse of breath drop in, and the rest of the production’s brief yet weighty 75 minutes is often very beautiful.
Unfortunately, though, the additions don't deepen Odets's play as much as bloat it in an attempt to hammer home the drivers' struggle as representative of all workers', then and now.
The abstraction clashes with Odets’ literal depictions of the working poor.
Sadly, the tepid revival at Classic Stage Company is unlikely to prompt a general strike.
Pasquale’s attempt to expand Waiting for Lefty is well intentioned, of course, but proves to be a fatal experiment.
This revival captures both the spirit of its time while offering an urgent warning to modern audiences.

cn.t: Odets' 1935 labor drama receives a mixed revival under first-time director Steven Pasquale, with critics finding the play's urgent message still resonant even as the production shows its age.

vr.q: This is a pretty successful exercise in elevating an otherwise cold and distant piece.
